back: A table that shows [[imp:classes (intervals) of data]] with a count of entries in each class.
The count is called the [[kw:frequency]] $ f $.
It helps organize large data sets to reveal patterns.

cards.front: Define [[kw:class width]] and how to compute it.
back: The distance between [[imp:lower limits of consecutive classes]].
Formula: $$\text{Class Width} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{Range}}{\text{Number of Classes}} \right\rceil$$
[[imp:Always round up]] to the next convenient number.
The difference between the [[imp:maximum and minimum]] data entries.
$$\text{Range} = \text{Max} - \text{Min}$$
Used to determine class width.
cards.front: What is the [[kw:range]] of a data set?

back: [[kw:Lower class limit]]: the [[imp:smallest value]] that can belong to a class.
[[kw:Upper class limit]]: the [[imp:largest value]] that can belong to a class.
Classes must not overlap and must cover all data.
cards.front: What are [[kw:lower class limit]] and [[kw:upper class limit]]?

back: The [[imp:representative value]] of a class.
Formula: $$\text{Midpoint} = \frac{\text{Lower Limit} + \text{Upper Limit}}{2}$$
Used in frequency polygons.
cards.front: What is the [[kw:midpoint]] of a class and how is it found?
Define [[kw:relative frequency]] and give its formula.
back: The [[imp:portion or percentage]] of data that falls in a class.
$$\text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{\text{Class Frequency } f}{\text{Sample Size } n}$$
Sum of relative frequencies is approximately 1 (or 100%).
The [[imp:running total]] of frequencies up to and including a class.
The cumulative frequency of the last class equals the total sample size $ n $.
Used to construct an ogive.
A bar graph where the horizontal scale is [[imp:quantitative (data values)]], vertical scale shows frequencies.
Consecutive bars must [[imp:touch]] because data are continuous.
Uses class boundaries, not limits.
Numbers that [[imp:separate classes without gaps]].
For integer data: lower boundary = lower limit − 0.5; upper boundary = upper limit + 0.5.
Example: class 59–114 → boundaries 58.5–114.5.
cards.front: What are [[kw:class boundaries]] and how do you find them for integer data?

back: A [[imp:line graph]] that plots frequency at each class midpoint, then connects points.
Extended to the horizontal axis one class width before first and after last class.
Shows the overall trend of the distribution.
Same shape as a frequency histogram, but the vertical scale shows [[imp:relative frequencies]] (proportions or percentages).
Useful for comparing distributions with different sample sizes.
A [[imp:cumulative frequency graph]] (line graph).
Plots cumulative frequency at each [[imp:upper class boundary]].
Always slopes upward from 0 to $ n $.
Steepest part shows the class with the greatest frequency.
cards.front: What is an [[kw:ogive]] and how is it constructed?
A data set has min=12, max=88, and you want 6 classes. What is the class width?
back: Class width = 13.
Quantitative data are [[imp:continuous]] — there are no gaps between possible values.
Gaps would falsely suggest that no data exist between classes.
Class boundaries ensure bars meet.
cards.front: Why must consecutive bars in a histogram touch?
Apply the blueprint: what are the steps to build a frequency distribution?
back: Understand: find min, max, range; decide number of classes.
Solve: compute class width (round up), set limits and boundaries, tally frequencies.
Solve: add midpoints, relative frequencies, cumulative frequencies.
Conclude: choose appropriate graph, interpret shape and patterns.
